'''Joseph Steven Madachy''' (March 16, 1927 – March 27, 2014) was a research chemist, technical editor and recreational mathematician. He was the lead editor of ''[[Journal of Recreational Mathematics]]''<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.baywood.com/edboard/rmed.asp?id=0022-412X|title=Journal of Recreational Mathematics|publisher=baywood.com|access-date=June 18, 2010}}</ref> for nearly 30 years and then served as editor emeritus. He was owner, publisher and editor of its predecessor, ''Recreational Mathematics Magazine,'' which appeared from 1961 to 1964.

== Early life and education ==
Madachy was born in Star Junction, Pennsylvania, to Steven and Anne Madachy.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.dignitymemorial.com/obituaries/dayton-oh/joseph-madachy-5910163|title=Joseph Steven Madachy Obituary - Dayton, OH|website=Dignity Memorial|language=en|access-date=2019-11-10}}</ref> He was raised in Cleveland, Ohio.<ref name=":0" /> He became interested in recreational mathematics after reading [[Eugene P. Northrop|Eugene Northrop]]'s 1944 book, ''Riddles in Mathematics''.<ref name=":1" /> After service in World War II, he attended [[Western Reserve University]] on the [[G.I. Bill]] and earned a bachelor's and a master's in Chemistry.<ref name=":0" />

== Career ==
Madachy moved to [[Dayton, Ohio|Dayton]], Ohio, and worked for [[Mound Laboratories]].<ref name=":0" /> He made original contributions to the field of recreational mathematics.<ref>[http://www.fq.math.ca/Scanned/6-1/madachy.pdf RECREATIONAL MATHEMATICS - The Fibonacci Quarterly]</ref> In 1960 he wrote to recreational mathematician [[Martin Gardner]], asking whether Gardner knew of any publications devoted solely to recreational mathematics, as he was considering starting such a project.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-eHqBgAAQBAJ&q=joseph+madachy&pg=PA271|title=Homage to a Pied Puzzler|last1=Schoen|first1=Alan|last2=Rodgers|first2=Tom|last3=Pegg|first3=Ed Jr.|date=2009-02-26|publisher=CRC Press|isbn=9781439865002|language=en}}</ref> Gardner responded in the negative, including a box containing his correspondence and suggesting Madachy could use the addresses to promote the magazine.<ref name=":2" /> From February 1961 to 1964 Madachy published the bimonthly ''Recreational Mathematics Magazine''.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Trigg|first=Charles W.|author-link=Charles W. Trigg|date=1 November 1961|title=Recreational Mathematics Magazine by Joseph Madachy|journal=Mathematics Magazine|language=en|volume=34|issue=7|pages=417–418|doi=10.2307/2687895|jstor=2687895}}</ref>[[File:Joseph Madachy - Mathematics on Vacation.jpg|thumb|left|Mathematics on Vacation]]

In 1967, [[Greenwood Press]] asked him to start the journal again under the title ''Journal of Recreational Mathematics,'' which was published by [[Baywood Publishing]] starting in 1973. He authored several books on recreational mathematics, including ''Mathematics on Vacation'' (1966),<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Liebeck|first=Pamela|author-link= Pamela Liebeck |date=1968|title=Mathematics on Vacation|url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/mathematical-gazette/article/mathematics-on-vacation-by-madachy-joseph-s-pp-251-695-1966-scribner/26E6334D4E290BA036A4C572B1DD98F5|journal=The Mathematical Gazette|language=en|volume=52|issue=382|pages=394|doi=10.2307/3611870|issn=0025-5572|jstor=3611870|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://www.kirkusreviews.com/book-reviews/joseph-s-madachy/mathematics-on-vacation/|title=Mathematics on Vacation by Joseph S. Madachy|date=14 November 1966|publisher=Kirkus Reviews|language=en}}</ref><ref>Joseph S. Madachy, ''Mathematics on Vacation'', Thomas Nelson & Sons Ltd. 1966</ref> ''Madachy's Mathematical Recreations''<ref>Madachy, J. S., ''Madachy's Mathematical Recreations'', New York: Dover, 1979.</ref> and ''Mathematical Diversions.''<ref>Hunter, J.A.H. and Madachy, J. S., ''Mathematical Diversions'', New York: Von Nostrand, 1963.</ref> He served as the literary agent for [[Dmitri Borgmann]]'s ''[[Language on Vacation]]''.<ref name="omni">{{cite journal |author=Scot Morris |date=October 1986 |title=Games |url=https://archive.org/details/omni-magazine-1986-10 |journal=[[Omni (magazine)|OMNI]] |volume=9 |issue=1 |pages=182–183 }}</ref> Longtime colleagues and co-authors include [[Martin Gardner]], [[Harry L. Nelson]], and [[Isaac Asimov]], and [[Solomon Golomb]] (with [[pentominos]]).

He worked with [[polyomino]]es,<ref name=":2" /> pentominos,<ref name="JRM1969">{{cite journal|title=Pentominos - Some Solved and Unsolved Problems |date=July 1969|journal=The Journal of Recreational Mathematics|publisher=Baywood Publishing}}</ref> [[prime number]]s,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://mathworld.wolfram.com/PrimeMagicSquare.html|title=Prime Magic Square|first=Eric W.|last=Weisstein|website=mathworld.wolfram.com}}</ref><ref>Madachy, J. S. "Magic and Antimagic Squares." Ch. 4 in Madachy's Mathematical Recreations. New York: Dover, pp. 85-113, 1979.</ref> and [[amicable numbers]]. He worked developing mathematical concepts such as [[cryptarithmetic]], used in cyber security applications.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://cryptarithms.awardspace.us/primer.html#MADACHY|title=A Primer on Cryptarithmetic|website=cryptarithms.awardspace.us}}</ref> He made contributions to Fibonacci series and [[narcissistic number]]s<ref>Joseph S. Madachy, ''Mathematics on Vacation'', Thomas Nelson & Sons Ltd. 1966, pages 163-175</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.magic-squares.net/narciss.htm|title=Narcissistic Numbers|website=www.magic-squares.net}}</ref><ref name="Fibonacci1972">{{cite journal|title=Some New Narcissistic Numbers|date=April 1972|journal=The Fibonacci Quarterly|publisher=The Fibonacci Association}}</ref> and devised puzzles using [[Fibonacci number]]s.<ref name="Fibonacci1968">{{cite journal |journal=The Fibonacci Quarterly|volume= 6| issue = 1|url=https://www.fq.math.ca/Scanned/6-1/madachy.pdf|title=Recreational mathematics|pages=60–68|access-date=20 June 2012|date=February 1968|publisher=The Fibonacci Association}}</ref>  His recreational mathematics work included areas in chess, [[magic square]]s<ref name="Pickover2003">{{cite book|last=Pickover|first=Clifford A.|title=The Zen of Magic Squares, Circles, and Stars: An Exhibition of Surprising Structures Across Dimensions|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9To1nPvY-1AC&pg=PA110|access-date=19 June 2012|date=2003-12-29|publisher=Princeton University Press|isbn=9780691115979|pages=110–}}</ref> and calculator art.<ref>"Calculator Art Contest", Journal of Recreational Mathematics, Baywood Publishing. July 1971</ref>

Madachy retired from editing ''Journal of Recreational Mathematics'' in 2000.<ref name=":2" />{{Rp|page=272}}[[File:Pentomino Puzzle Solutions.svg|thumb|Pentomino Puzzle Solutions]]

==In popular culture==

Madachy is mentioned in the [[Jack Reacher]] novel series in the book ''[[Never Go Back (Lee Child novel)|Never Go Back]],'' which uses [[perfect digit-to-digit invariant]] numbers in the plot: "Such numbers had been much discussed by a guy called Joseph Madachy, who once upon a time had been the owner, publisher, and editor of a magazine called Journal of Recreational Mathematics."

== Personal life ==
Madachy and his wife, Juliana, lived in Dayton, Ohio and had six children.<ref name=":0" />
